analysis.one_liner: Makes ethanol and biodiesel fuel tax credits and ethanol import tariffs permanent.
analysis.headline: Despite 18 bipartisan cosponsors, the bill never left the House Ways and Means Committee and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have removed the expiration dates on federal tax credits for ethanol and biodiesel, making them permanent, and would have made the tariff on imported ethanol take effect immediately with no end date. The credits go mainly to fuel blenders and producers, and the tariff keeps cheaper foreign ethanol — mainly Brazilian sugarcane ethanol — out of the U.S. market. Costs would fall on taxpayers through forgone revenue and on fuel buyers through the tariff.
analysis.who_benefits: Corn ethanol producers and the fuel blenders who claim the credit would gain a permanent subsidy rather than one Congress must renew every year or two. Biodiesel and renewable diesel producers would gain the same permanence for their credit. A permanent tariff with no expiration date would shield the domestic ethanol industry from lower-priced imported ethanol indefinitely.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ethanol and biodiesel producers and blenders

how_it_helps.text: Makes the income tax credit for alcohol (ethanol) used as fuel permanent by striking the subsection that ends it.
Makes the income tax credit for biodiesel and renewable diesel used as fuel permanent.
Makes the excise tax credits for alcohol fuel mixtures and biodiesel mixtures permanent, removing their expiration dates.
Rewrites the ethanol tariff lines of the Harmonized Tariff Schedule so that duties on imported ethyl alcohol take effect immediately on enactment and have no sunset date.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would bear the permanently forgone revenue from the ethanol and biodiesel credits, which would no longer come up for periodic review. Drivers and fuel buyers would pay through the permanent tariff, which blocks cheaper imported ethanol — chiefly Brazilian sugarcane ethanol — from entering the market.

drawbacks.text: Making the ethanol and biodiesel credits permanent removes the expiration dates that currently force Congress to periodically reconsider them, locking in the revenue cost with no offset.

Making the tariff on imported ethanol effective immediately and permanent keeps lower-priced foreign ethanol out of the U.S. market, raising costs for blenders and ultimately for drivers, and cuts against the bill's own energy-supply goal.

The bill contains no mechanism to steer support away from mature corn ethanol toward emerging renewable fuels, so the permanent subsidy would flow to an established industry regardless of performance.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concentrated: a permanent annual subsidy stream for the ethanol and biodiesel industries and permanent protection from import competition. The costs are diffuse but real — billions in forgone federal revenue over time and somewhat higher fuel costs from the tariff. Even a supporter of renewable fuels could object to making these credits permanent with no fiscal offset and no performance review, since permanence is precisely what removes Congress's leverage to reform or redirect the subsidies later.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a markup, or a vote before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Earl Pomeroy introduced the bill on January 4, 2007, joined by Rep. Kenny Hulshof, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
Eighteen members cosponsored the bill — 11 Democrats and 7 Republicans.
The Ways and Means Committee took no action beyond the referral; the bill received no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote, and it died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Taxpayers and drivers are better off because the bill died: the ethanol and biodiesel credits stayed subject to periodic renewal instead of becoming permanent, and no permanent tariff wall against cheaper imported ethanol was enacted. The ethanol and biodiesel industries did not get the permanence they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers and drivers at the pump

for.name: Earl Pomeroy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited cosponsors; his state is a major ethanol producer.

for.name: Kenny Hulshof
for.what_they_did: Joined Pomeroy in introducing the bill on day one.

for.name: Ethanol and corn producer interests
for.what_they_did: Long pushed Congress to make ethanol tax credits and the import tariff permanent rather than subject to periodic renewal.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction (chaired by Charles Rangel, D-NY)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no markup was scheduled in the two years it had jurisdiction, so it never reached the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was bipartisan (11 Democrats and 7 Republicans), but the bill never came to a vote, so no roll-call shows how the parties would have lined up.

industries.note: The bill would make the ethanol tax credits and the import tariff permanent, guaranteeing the industry both a permanent subsidy and permanent protection from cheaper Brazilian sugarcane ethanol. The cost — forgone federal revenue and somewhat higher fuel prices — falls on taxpayers and drivers.
Their tax credit would become permanent instead of requiring periodic renewal. The subsidy supports a renewable fuel, but permanence removes Congress's ability to reassess its cost or effectiveness.

industries.industry: Fuel blenders (largely oil refiners and marketers)
industries.note: Blenders claim the alcohol and biodiesel mixture excise credits, so permanence is a permanent revenue stream for them — but the permanent tariff would raise their cost on any imported ethanol they use.

The tariff would apply immediately and never expire, keeping their lower-priced ethanol out of the U.S. market. Their exclusion is what allows domestic ethanol prices to stay higher than the world price.
